Title: Empowering patients through support and information
NewsSummary: New website will address myths and stigmas related to advanced stages of breast cancer.
NewsContent:
Metastatic Breast Cancer (MBC) patients can now access a comprehensive website  containing up-to-date information and resources on how to fight the disease and enhance the recovery process. 

Launched by the Kenyan Metastatic Breast Cancer Network (KMBCN) in partnership with Aga Khan University, the website will meet the needs of patients by acting as a central point for information on virtual support groups, news about clinical trials, nearby health facilities, educational videos, and advice columns on exercise, diet and lifestyle. 

The burden of breast cancer is a major public health concern in Africa since as many as three in four patients in the region suffer from late stages of the disease. Research also indicates that many women with MBC suffer from clinical depression and anxiety, and four out of five of these women do not receive any services, referral or guidance. 

Patients will be able to share inspiring stories of their journey through cancer treatment and learn about research updates or support events.  Regular surveys and question-and-answers sessions on the website will also ensure that the portal evolves to meet patient needs.

Speaking at the launch ceremony, Dr Asim Jamal Shaikh, associate professor and head of the medical oncology division at the Aga Khan University Hospital in Nairobi, and the project lead, said the website would dispel myths and address stigmas about breast cancer that would help alleviate the physical and emotional toll of the disease.

"By designing a website that is centered on user needs, we will provide relevant information that empowers patients and enables them to cope with their challenges," Dr Shaikh added.  

Funded through a SPARC grant, a global competition run by the Union of International Cancer Control, an advocacy group which represents the world's major cancer societies, ministries of health and patient communities, the information collected through the website is in line with the goals  of the Kenyan Health Ministry's National Cancer Control Strategy 2017-2022.  

The data and research from local communities that lead to policy and planning are crucial in alleviating a nation's suffering from cancer, Dr Shaikh added. "There are important research generating and data collection tools incorporated within this web platform."

Also present at the occasion was Dr Alfred Karagu, CEO, National Cancer Institute of Kenya (NCI), the coordinating body for all cancer control activities in the country, who said the website would address gaps in care provision by providing reliable information to patients. Dr Karagu said that with a majority of Kenyans having access to internet in the region and a high percentage of literate women in the country, the forum will go a long way towards improving their quality of life. 

Meanwhile, Professor Robert Armstrong, founding dean of the Medical College in East Africa, said the website would be an invaluable resource for research in line with Aga Khan University's vision and hoped it would contribute positively towards addressing the needs of cancer patients. 

The project will see Dr Shaikh collaborate with several other public and private hospitals, cancer support groups, NCI, Kenya Society of Haematology and Oncology, Kenyan Network of Cancer Organizations and other cancer care centres in Kenya to assess and meet the needs of the country's breast cancer patients.

The website's vision matches targets under goal 3 of the global Sustainable Development Goals:  ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all at all ages that call for steps to improve mental health and to tackle the burden of non-communicable diseases such as cancer.
